https://www.dw.com/en/german-army-helps-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JEG6 The German army is helping Poland strengthen the East Shield, for example by installing anti-tank obstacles Image: Polnische Streitkräfte/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Poland started to construct a defensive barrier along its border with Russia and Belarus in 2024. The East Shield defense system will eventually be around 800 kilometers long, and is intended to protect this country on NATO's eastern flank against attack from the east. When the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk , inspected the first completed section in November 2024, he declared that the project was meant to "deter and discourage a potential aggressor" and was "truly an investment in peace." The Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 was a profound shock to Poland's sense of security. The Tusk government has increased defense spending in 2026 to 200 billion zlotys (around 46 billion euros, or 54 billion dollars) ― almost 5% of Poland's GDP. This means that, in relative terms, Poland has the highest defense spending of all the members of NATO . The government has also bought the most advanced weapons available, particularly from the US, and is proceeding with the construction of the East Shield, a complex defense system along its eastern border. A shield against Russia Since June, around 40 German sappers, or combat engineers, have been helping to establish the defenses. The German army's combat engineer unit is specially trained in blocking the movement of enemy troops. The sappers are currently deployed near Budry in Masuria, close to the border with Russia. The fence marking the border is visible from where they are working, partially obscured by a row of trees on the Polish side. The German soldiers are installing anti-tank obstacles to impede battle tanks in the event of an attack. A yellow backhoe loader lifts the spiky concrete blocks, known as Czech hedgehogs, off a truck and places them on the muddy ground. This installation, around 200 meters back from the border, consists of three rows of these concrete blocks. A deep ditch and another line of hedgehogs run along the border itself. A Polish officer explains that mines can quickly be laid in the zone between the two lines of Czech hedgehogs. "The German sappers have done an excellent job," the Polish general Stanislaw Czosnek said when he inspected the works on Thursday. He added that he was "very impressed" by his German colleagues' performance. In the six weeks since their deployment, the German engineers have laid more than a kilometer of blocks. "We stand ready to fight for democracy and freedom," stressed the German general Tito Gante, who accompanied Czosnek on the inspection. He praised the comradely atmosphere between the German and the Polish soldiers. The Bundeswehr has declared its support for the East Shield an official mission: "We want to maintain peace with a credible deterrent," Gante said. The German contingent will stay until October, but the sappers will soon be deployed at other sections of the East Shield. The work near Budry is due to be completed over the coming week. The anti-tank obstacles can only be moved by a backhoe loader Image: Jacek Lepiarz/DW Politically symbolic "Above all, the participation of German sappers has politically symbolic significance," Lukasz Jasinski, an analyst at the Polish Institute for International Affairs, told DW. "Poland wants to convince Germany and other partners that Poland's eastern border is also the external border of the EU and NATO. Our Western partners should treat this border a bit like their own." Poland and Germany were quick to establish military cooperation after the end of the Cold War. Later, when Poland joined NATO in 1999, this created the necessary political and institutional conditions for close collaboration . Since then, NATO's Multinational Corps Northeast , in which Poland and Germany both have leading roles, has been headquartered in the Polish city of Szczecin. In 2003, Germany sold the MiG-29 fighter jets it inherited from the former East German Air Force to Poland for the symbolic price of one euro each. Joint military exercises and exchange programs for both officers and soldiers are now standard practice. When Russia attacked Ukraine in February 2022, there were initial tensions between Germany and Poland on account of the cautious response from Berlin. Overall, though, the attack has further strengthened cooperation between the two. The Bundeswehr has supported Polish air defense by supplying several units of the Patriot air defense system, with their German crews. German fighter jets are helping to protect Polish air space, most recently as part of the NATO mission Enhanced Air Policing North (eAPN) in Malbork. A German air force Eurofighter Typhoon taking off in December 2025 from the Polish military airbase in Malbork Image: Adam Warøawa/PAP/dpa/picture alliance Questions of military cooperation were also prioritized in the closing statement that followed German-Polish intergovernmental consultations on December 1, 2025. The process culminated in the signing of the German-Polish defense agreement on June 17, 2026. On August 15 this year, three German planes, two Eurofighters and an A400M transport aircraft, participated in the celebration of Polish Armed Forces Day. The head of the German air force, Holger Neumann, was one of the guests of honor. Some American GIs marched in the military parade ― but no German soldiers. Kaczynski: No German soldiers in Poland However, not all the political forces in Poland are happy about this new Polish-German brotherhood-in-arms. Memories of the trauma of World War II are still very much alive in Polish society and are regularly instrumentalized by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) to stir up anti-German feeling. Back in 2014, PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski said he didn't want any German soldiers in Poland. "It will be at least seven generations before that is acceptable," he said. The line of anti-tank obstacles forming part of the East Shield near Budry in Poland Image: Jacek Lepiarz/DW In the fall of 2022, when the German government offered to relocate two German Patriot batteries to Poland after an incident involving a Ukrainian rocket gone astray, the PiS government blocked the move. "Germany's previous behavior gives us no reason to believe that it will decide to fire on the Russian rockets," Kaczynski declared. Just last March, Poland's president Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by the PiS, vetoed legislation that would have allowed Poland to access almost 44 billion euros (55 billion dollars) in EU defense loans because German armaments companies could also have benefited. Poland sees the US as the most important guarantor of its security, and is trying to establish a special relationship with Washington. Around 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in various places around the country. Warsaw is keen to establish a permanent military base on its territory: Until now, a significant number of the US soldiers are in Poland on rotation. This article has been translated from German. Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/Reuters Iran Trump planning new military assault or tighter sanctions, say Iranian officials Regime adviser says Tehran could be forced into pre-emptive strikes if stalemate continues Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Wed 11 Nov 2026 13.47 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 16.03 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Senior Iranian officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an ever-tightening economic stranglehold that will push Tehran into retaliatory action. The assessment comes from Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. Mohammadi said on his Telegram channel that the Americans had proposed a timeframe of about two weeks after which Donald Trump would make a decision on military action. Mohammadi, who is regarded as a reliable indicator of Ghalibaf’s thinking, cast doubt on the US president’s claim that the military option was off the table . He claimed Washington was preparing for a limited strike and Iran was already preparing a response. If the US sanctions continued, he said, a comprehensive pre-emptive war would be needed “to increase the cost of sanctions for the enemy”. Mohammadi described the US response to Iran’s latest proposals on reopening the strait of Hormuz as “not only unsatisfactory but completely deceptive”. “They do not want to release the frozen funds,” he said. “They do not want to lift the sanctions and they do not want to stop the war in Lebanon.” He also disclosed that Iran had rejected a request from the US vice-president, JD Vance, for a direct meeting with its negotiators before giving a response to Tehran’s conditions for lifting the siege on the strait. For now, Trump has settled on a strategy of suffocating Iran through economic pressure and tightening the blockade on its oil exports while facilitating those of other Gulf states through Hormuz. View image in fullscreen A tanker burns off Oman in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, apparently after an attack by Iranian forces trying to stop oil shipments. Photograph: Social media/Reuters Mohammadi’s assessments suggest some senior Iranians fear Washington’s strategy might work by destabilising the country. The thinking goes that economic turmoil might spark street protests, potentially around the anniversary of nationwide demonstrations that began in late December last year. On this basis, the Iranian leadership might conclude that the status quo – a “no peace, no war” impasse – was not sustainable and pre-emptive action was required. Despite Iranian claims that their blockade of the strait is working, there is concern that Brent crude is at a relatively low $93 a barrel, while Saudi oil production is near prewar levels of 9.3m barrels a day. In an attempt to close any loopholes, Iran said it bombed a US radar post on the Omani island of Didamar three days ago. In another development, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s national security council, said he had told Russia that Iran was not prepared for even a particle of its highly enriched stockpile of uranium to leave the country, saying it might be needed for planned nuclear-powered submarines. A third senior official, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, warned Europe that any complicity in the US blockade would be “an act of war that will be etched in the nation’s historical memory”. Tehran has been increasingly clear that US bases in Europe will be targeted if fighting resumes. Rezaei said: “If American planes take off from a distant military base and come to this country to bomb Iran, we will also target that base. We are announcing this now so they have no excuse tomorrow.” Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, gave the impression this week that the policy of economic strangulation was sufficient and described Iran’s demands as unrealistic. However, Trump is under pressure to resolve the crisis before the Democrats take charge of Congress on 3 January. A Reuters Ipsos poll in the US shows 71% of Americans want Congress to pass legislation to end the war in Iran. The overwhelming message from the midterm elections was that the conflict was highly unpopular but the Democrats do not have a strategy to end it and open up the strait of Hormuz. This risks leaving the political initiative with the White House, and an increasingly hardline Iranian leadership.
